rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 4-5 report the authors' own dataset (429 UAV RGB images from three olive fields in northern Greece, Oct-Nov 2022, 3038 annotated tree instances) and their own training/testing of YOLOv5n/s/m at two input sizes, with precision, recall and mAP results (Fig. 6, Tables 5-6).
rows.notes: The study only shows that YOLOv5 applied to UAV RGB imagery can detect olive trees and classify them as healthy or damaged by Verticillium wilt, with the medium 640x640 model performing best; the damaged class scored consistently lower. It does not report any result on controlling the pathogen's expansion (the claimed function, pest_control) nor on early detection: images were taken when symptoms are most pronounced and classes were based on visibly altered canopy colour; early detection with thermal/NIR imagery is listed only as future work. Detection is a precondition of control, so upstream is set. Note also the study concerns Verticillium dahliae, not Xylella fastidiosa as in the review's context, although the technology (UAV remote sensing) is the same. No triangulation (single method), no mechanism, single region/crop, field-scale only, no stated requirements, limitations mentioned only loosely (few training images, class imbalance) and no dispersion measures for the metrics.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a methodological object-detection paper on Verticillium wilt detection in olive trees; the review cites it in a context about Xylella fastidiosa control and early detection, which the study does not address.
